steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on unsupervised multi-person 3D human pose estimation from 2D poses alone. It should explain why lifting several people at once is hard for existing unsupervised methods and state what the paper sets out to do.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Monocular 3D HPE is ill-posed; unsupervised single-person lifting progress
- Depth ambiguity and the root-joint / fixed-distance workaround
- Why this breaks for multiple people
- Aim of the paper and novelty

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Monocular 3D HPE
  - ill-posed inverse problem: many different 2D poses -> same 3D pose
  - still, unsupervised single-person 2D-3D HPE from single image developing rapidly (cite)
  - lift 2D skeleton to 3D via some reprojected 2D pose likelihood
- Depth ambiguity
  - fundamental perspective ambiguity -> no absolute metric of depth from single view (cite)
  - workaround: centre detected 2D pose on root joint (typically pelvis)
  - 3D prediction of root set to fixed unit c from camera
  - so models predict 3D depth offset from root, root assumed c units away
- Multi-person problem
  - fine for lifting one person
  - adapt to several people simultaneously -> errors in pose and in 3D distance between the two people (Fig. 1)
- Aim / novelty
  - accurate reconstruction of interacting 3D poses in shared coordinate system
  - only 2D poses from a single image
  - extensive literature survey: no prior work on unsupervised multi-person 2D-3D HPE from 2D poses alone
  - first leap: is it feasible to reconstruct accurate 3D estimate of two people interacting from 2D poses alone

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Monocular 3D human pose estimation (HPE) is an ill-posed inverse problem, because multiple different 2D poses can correspond to the same 3D pose. Even so, unsupervised algorithms for single-person 2D-3D HPE from a single image have developed quickly. These algorithms try to lift a 2D skeleton to 3D using some kind of reprojected 2D pose likelihood. But because of the fundamental perspective ambiguity, the absolute metric of depth can't be obtained from just a single view. To deal with this, unsupervised approaches centre the detected 2D pose around a root joint (usually the pelvis), and they also set the 3D prediction of the root to be a fixed unit of c away from the camera. So the models don't learn absolute depth, instead they learn to predict the 3D depth offset from the root joint, when the root is assumed to be c units from the camera.

- adapting the root-centred approach to several people at once -> errors in the pose and in the 3D distance between the two people (Fig. 1)
- aim: accurate reconstruction of 3D poses interacting in a shared coordinate system, only from 2D poses from a single image
- survey of prior literature: no prior work on unsupervised multi-person 2D-3D HPE from 2D poses alone
- first leap: feasible to reconstruct accurate 3D estimate of two interacting people from 2D poses alone?

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Monocular 3D human pose estimation (HPE) is an ill-posed inverse problem, because multiple different 2D poses can correspond to the same 3D pose. Even so, unsupervised algorithms for single-person 2D-3D HPE from a single image have developed quickly. These algorithms try to lift a 2D skeleton to 3D using some kind of reprojected 2D pose likelihood. But because of the fundamental perspective ambiguity, the absolute metric of depth can't be obtained from just a single view. To deal with this, unsupervised approaches centre the detected 2D pose around a root joint (usually the pelvis), and they also set the 3D prediction of the root to be a fixed unit of c away from the camera. So the models don't learn absolute depth, instead they learn to predict the 3D depth offset from the root joint, when the root is assumed to be c units from the camera.

This works well when we only want to lift a single person. But if we adapt this approach to lift multiple people at the same time we get errors in the pose, and also errors in the 3D distance between the two people, as seen in Fig. 1. So the aim of this paper is to get an accurate reconstruction of 3D human poses interacting within a shared coordinate system, using only their 2D poses obtained from a single image. Also, we did an extensive survey of the prior literature and we found no prior work that tackles unsupervised multi-person 2D-3D HPE from 2D poses alone. So we take the first leap in exploring if it is feasible to reconstruct an accurate 3D estimate of two people interacting from only their 2D poses.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
Monocular 3D human pose estimation (HPE) is an ill-posed inverse problem, because multiple different 2D poses can correspond to the same 3D pose. Even so, unsupervised algorithms for single-person 2D-3D HPE from a single image have developed quickly. These algorithms try to lift a 2D skeleton to 3D using some kind of reprojected 2D pose likelihood [1,2,3,4,5]. But because of the fundamental perspective ambiguity, the absolute metric of depth can't be obtained from just a single view [3,6]. To deal with this, unsupervised approaches centre the detected 2D pose around a root joint (usually the pelvis), and they also set the 3D prediction of the root to be a fixed unit of c away from the camera. So the models don't learn absolute depth, instead they learn to predict the 3D depth offset from the root joint, when the root is assumed to be c units from the camera.

This works well when we only want to lift a single person. But if we adapt this approach to lift multiple people at the same time we get errors in the pose, and also errors in the 3D distance between the two people, as seen in Fig. 1. So the aim of this paper is to get an accurate reconstruction of 3D human poses interacting within a shared coordinate system, using only their 2D poses obtained from a single image. Also, we did an extensive survey of the prior literature and we found no prior work that tackles unsupervised multi-person 2D-3D HPE from 2D poses alone. So we take the first leap in exploring if it is feasible to reconstruct an accurate 3D estimate of two people interacting from only their 2D poses.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Monocular 3D human pose estimation (HPE) is known to be an ill-posed inverse problem, since multiple different 2D poses can correspond to the same 3D pose. Despite this, unsupervised algorithms have developed rapidly in tackling single-person 2D-3D HPE from a single image, where they try to lift a 2D skeleton to 3D via some form of reprojected 2D pose likelihood [1,2,3,4,5]. However, due to fundamental perspective ambiguity, the absolute metric of depth cannot be obtained from a single view alone [3,6]. To deal with this, unsupervised approaches centre the detected 2D pose around a root joint (typically the pelvis), and also set the 3D prediction of the root to be a fixed unit of c from the camera. This means that rather than absolute depth, these models learn to predict the 3D depth offset from the root joint when the root is assumed to be c units from the camera. While this works well when we want to lift a single person, if we adapt this approach to lift multiple people simultaneously we obtain errors both in the pose and in the 3D distance between the two people, as seen in Fig. 1. The aim of this paper is therefore to obtain an accurate reconstruction of 3D human poses interacting within a shared coordinate system, relying only on their 2D poses obtained from a single image. In addition, our extensive survey of prior literature found no prior work tackling unsupervised multi-person 2D-3D HPE from 2D poses alone. We therefore take the first leap in exploring whether it is feasible to reconstruct an accurate 3D estimate of two people interacting from their 2D poses alone.

References:

[2] Bastian Wandt, James J. Little, and Helge Rhodin. Elepose: Unsupervised 3d human pose estimation by predicting camera elevation and learning normalizing flows on 2d poses. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) , pages 6635–6645, 2022.
[3] Ching-Hang Chen, Ambrish Tyagi, Amit Agrawal, Dylan Drover, Rohith MV, Stefan Stojanov, and James M. Rehg. Unsupervised 3d pose estimation with geometric self-supervision. In 2019 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) , pages 5707–5717, 2019.
